title: Materials management
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:35Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: None of the bank points teaches materials management: forecasting demand, the master production schedule, materials requirement planning and just-in-time inventory control. The closest cards cover operations in general or supply chain logistics, which are broader than this point.

draft.title: Materials management
card: Materials management aims to have the right materials in the right amount at the right time, without waste or running short.
predicting how much customers will buy. It guides how much the business plans to make.
a plan of what will be made, how many, and when, based on the forecast. Materials requirement planning (MRP) then works out which materials are needed and when to order them.
ordering materials to arrive just as they are needed. It cuts the cost of storing stock, but delays from suppliers can stop production.
draft.remember: Forecast, schedule, plan materials, and order them to arrive when needed.

a.q: What does a master production schedule set out?
opts: What will be made, how many, and when
How much customers are predicted to buy
Which suppliers offer the lowest prices
Materials delivered only as they are used
a.why: The schedule is the plan for what to make, how many and when. Predicting what customers will buy is forecasting, which the schedule is based on, so it is the tempting wrong choice.
a.clue: It is a plan for production, made after the forecast.

b.q: Leila's Geelong bike shop assembles bikes from parts it orders to arrive on the day each batch is built. What is the main risk of this approach?
opts: A late supplier delivery could stop assembly
Large amounts of money are tied up in stored parts
Customer demand can no longer be forecast
Bikes must be made before any orders are planned
b.why: Ordering parts to arrive as needed is just-in-time. With little stock held, a late delivery can stop production. High storage costs are the problem just-in-time reduces, not one it creates.
b.clue: Think about what happens when there is no spare stock.

a.best: What will be made, how many, and when

b.best: A late supplier delivery could stop assembly
